title: Customs, guests and Tsagaan Sar
goal: Understanding the Mongolian customs that matter most for guests — and mastering the polite phrases that get you welcomed, not just tolerated.
bekal: behave correctly as a guest in a home and in a ger
say the Tsagaan Sar greetings and answer them
use respectful language: *та*, *хүндэтгэл*, and the right forms of address

dialogs.title: Яриа — Цагаан сарын мэнд
dialogs.intro: The first day of Tsagaan Sar. Budi is invited to Sarnai's grandparents' home on the edge of town. It's his first meeting with the most senior person in the family.

notes: ⚠️ **Золгох is the special Tsagaan Sar greeting, and it has no equivalent anywhere.** The younger person holds out both arms **underneath**, palms up, supporting the elder's elbows; the elder places their arms **on top**. Then the two kiss each other's cheeks or touch foreheads. Age, not rank, decides who is on top.

**Амар байна уу? is the Tsagaan Sar greeting, not an everyday one.** Literally "is it peaceful?", and the answer is simply a repeat: *Амар, амар.* ⚠️ Using it outside Tsagaan Sar sounds like saying "Merry Christmas" in September.
**Сар шинэдээ сайхан шинэлж байна уу? is the set phrase you'll hear dozens of times over the three days of Tsagaan Sar.** The answer: *Сайхан шинэлж байна, таныг ч бас.* Learn both as one chunk.

**Бүү is an older, gentler prohibition than битгий.** *Хоосон **бүү** суу* = "don't sit empty-handed". You'll hear it from older people and in proverbs; the *битгий* you learned in unit 10 is the everyday form.

**Хүү минь literally means "my son" and is used as an affectionate address for any young man**, not just one's own son. Its English equivalent is "son" or "lad". For a young woman: *охин минь*. ⚠️ If someone calls you this, you've been accepted.

grammars.title: Respectful language: what changes and what doesn't
body: Mongolian **has no layered speech levels like Japanese or Korean**. There are just a few word choices, and most politeness is shown through behavior, not grammar. That's good news for beginners.

head: Plain
Respectful
Meaning
Note
rows: The most important one. Use *та* when unsure.

after: ⚠️ **Of this whole table, only the first two rows are truly essential at A1.** The rest you just need to recognize when you hear them. Using *та* correctly covers ninety percent of Mongolian verbal politeness.

**Far more important than word choice is behavior:** receiving with both hands, not refusing tea, not stepping on the threshold, and letting elders go first. Mongolians forgive messy grammar without a second thought; what they notice is your hands.

grammars.title: Wishes and congratulations
body: Mongolian is rich in wishes, and most are formed with the suffix **-ье / -ъя** (let's) or the word **хүсье** (I wish).

head: Монгол
Say it
When to say it
rows: Tsagaan Sar greeting, to an elder.

after: ⚠️ **Мэнд хүргэе literally means "I send greetings" and pairs with almost any celebration.** *Наадмын мэнд хүргэе* (happy Naadam), *баярын мэнд хүргэе* (happy holiday). A pattern that saves a lot of memorizing.

**Хүсье means "I wish" and goes at the end of the wish.** *Амжилт хүсье* (good luck), *эрүүл мэнд хүсье* (wishing you health). Notice that the thing wished comes first, following the SOV order you've already mastered.

blocks.text: **Цагаан сар** (tsa-GAAN sar) is the Mongolian Lunar New Year, falling between late January and early March. It's the biggest celebration of the year, and the idea will feel familiar to anyone who knows Christmas or Lunar New Year: **everyone goes home to family, visits their elders and eats too much for three days.**

head: Монгол
Say it
What it is
rows: The eve of Tsagaan Sar. Eat until completely full; leaving leftovers is bad luck.
The first day. Get up before sunrise and visit your elders.
The special greeting with supported arms.
A tower of layered biscuits on the table. The number of layers is always odd.
A whole boiled sheep's back — the main dish.
Thousands of dumplings made weeks in advance and frozen outdoors.
A blue silk scarf held during zolgokh; blue = sky.
Gifts. Every guest goes home with something.

blocks.title: ⚠️ If you're invited to Tsagaan Sar
items: **Bring a small gift for the host** — chocolate, tea, a scarf. Its value doesn't matter; the gesture does.
**You'll eat at many homes in one day.** By the fourth home you won't manage much; still taste a sip of tea and a small bite. Refusing completely is the only real mistake.
**Small cash gifts for children and elders are common** — much like red envelopes at Lunar New Year.
**Don't greet anyone younger than you with zolgokh.** Your arms will be the wrong way round and everyone will notice.

sections.title: Customs to know before you visit

head: Custom
Why
rows: **Receive anything with your right hand, supported at the elbow by your left.**
The left hand alone is seen as dismissive. This is the custom people notice most.
**Taste the tea or milk you're offered.**
Tea is the home's sign of welcome; refusing it refuses the home.
In old belief, the threshold guards the home.
**Don't point at people or the fire with your index finger.**
Use your whole hand, palm up.
**If you bump someone's foot, shake hands at once.**
A handshake cancels the slip instantly.
**Don't pour water or milk onto the fire.**
Fire is the spirit of the household.
It's believed to call up wind and spirits.
**Don't leave food uneaten on Битүүн night.**
An empty plate means a year of plenty.

blocks.text: Notice that **many of these customs have twins across Asia and beyond** — the right hand for giving and receiving, no pointing with the index finger, elders first, never refusing what's offered. If they're new to you, don't worry: **this table is your shortcut, and simply trying earns you a great deal of goodwill.**

head: Монгол
Say it
English
rows: sacred stone cairn on a hilltop

blocks.text: ⚠️ **An овоо is a cairn of stones on a hilltop or at a crossroads**, often decorated with blue cloth and bones. When you pass one, the custom is to **walk around it three times clockwise** while adding a stone. Long-distance bus drivers often stop for this. Join in — it's free, quick and appreciated.

blocks.title: Ten polite sentences that open doors
items: *Танилцахад таатай байна.* — Nice to meet you.
*Урьсанд баярлалаа.* — Thank you for inviting me.
*Гэр тань маш сайхан байна.* — Your home is lovely.
*Хоол маш амттай байна.* — The food is delicious.
*Уучлаарай, би сайн ойлгосонгүй.* — Sorry, I didn't quite understand.
*Дахин хэлж өгнө үү.* — Could you say that again, please?
*Та маш сайн хүн байна.* — You're a very kind person.
*Их баярлалаа, дараа дахин уулзая.* — Thank you so much, see you again.
*Сайн яваарай.* — Take care on your way.
